tips.title: A leitmotif has to be tied to something
tips.body: Any tune can come back. A **leitmotif** is a short idea attached to a **character, a place or an idea**, which returns and changes as the story does. Calling every recurring theme a leitmotif without saying what it is attached to is the commonest way to lose the mark.

tips.title: Ask whether the characters can hear it
tips.body: A radio in the room, a band in the bar, a character humming — that is **diegetic** music, part of the scene. An orchestra nobody on screen can hear is **non-diegetic** score. The same tune can be both, and a film that moves it from one to the other is doing something worth writing about.

tips.title: Describe the interval, not the feeling
tips.body: A rising **perfect fifth** sounds open and confident; a **tritone** points nowhere and sounds unstable; a **minor third** darkens. Naming the interval and then the effect is one point made properly. Naming only the effect is half a point at best.

tips.title: Say how the motif changed, not that it did
tips.body: Transposed, inverted, in retrograde, augmented, in diminution, fragmented, reharmonised, given to a different instrument, moved into the minor. Nine named things, each of which can be heard and credited. **It comes back different** cannot.

why.matters: Film music is not decoration. Before a word is spoken it has told you where you are and how to feel, it names a character before they appear, it carries you across a cut, and it marks the moment the story turns. A leitmotif is the device that does most of that work: a short idea attached to a person or an idea, which returns when they do and changes as the story changes them. The exam asks not what is happening in the music but what it is doing for the film, and this topic is the vocabulary for saying so.

examples.title: The corridor scene
examples.body: One shot: someone walks down a corridor. Put low sustained strings with a tremolo under it and it is dread. Put a bassoon and pizzicato strings under it and it is a comedy. Put a slow solo piano in a minor key under it and someone has died. The picture did not change. The cue did, and the audience felt whatever the cue told them to feel. That is the job people notice least and composers work hardest at, and it is why *what is the music doing* is the exam's question.

visual.alt: A table of three cues placed under one unchanged shot of a corridor, low tremolo strings, pizzicato and bassoon, or a slow minor piano, and the different feeling each one gives the audience

examples.title: The theme that arrives before the character
examples.body: A single horn plays a few quiet notes and the audience knows who is about to walk in. That is a leitmotif doing its job, and three things make it possible: it is short, three to seven notes; it has one striking interval or rhythm that makes it unmistakable; and it survives being changed. The last is what matters. The same theme slow and quiet on one horn means something quite different from the full brass at the start, and it means it *because* you recognise it.

boxes.title: Full brass, loud
boxes.body: The hero arrives: the theme at full strength.

boxes.title: One horn, slow and quiet
boxes.body: A memory of the hero, or a doubt about them.

boxes.title: In the minor
boxes.body: One note in each chord moved, and the same theme is now a threat.

boxes.title: Fragmented
boxes.body: Only the first interval, repeated, never completing: tension.

visual.alt: Four boxes showing one leitmotif in four states, on full brass, on a single quiet horn, in the minor and fragmented, each recognisable and each meaning something different

examples.title: The ringtone and the jingle
examples.body: A phone's ringtone and a shop's jingle are leitmotifs with a job: a few notes that identify their owner across a room, still recognisable when muffled by a bag or played on a different phone. They obey the same three rules as a film theme, short, one distinctive shape, survives change, because those rules are what make a musical idea stick to a thing. The development techniques are the same too: the jingle in a minor key is the joke version, and everyone gets the joke because they know the original.

steps.title: What film music is for
steps.body:
Film music is not decoration. It is doing specific jobs, and an answer that names the job is already half written.

**Establishing a world.** Before a word is spoken, the music tells you where and when you are. A full late-Romantic orchestra says *epic*; a solo shakuhachi says somewhere quite different; a synthesiser says the future, or at least a particular idea of it.

**Telling you how to feel.** The same shot of someone walking down a corridor is suspense, comedy or grief depending entirely on the cue underneath it. This is the job people notice least and the composer works hardest at.

**Identifying a character or idea.** A short musical idea attached to a person, a place or a concept — a **leitmotif** — lets the music tell you who is coming before you see them, and comment on them when you do.

**Holding the film together.** Music covers cuts, joins scenes that were shot months apart, and carries the audience over a jump in time or place. Without it a film falls into pieces.

**Marking a moment.** A **stinger** is a sharp chord or crash timed exactly to something on screen. So is the older, more literal technique of **mickey-mousing**, where the music follows the action step for step — footsteps in the bassoon, a fall in a descending glissando.

Every one of these is a sentence you can write in an exam, and each becomes an answer when a musical feature is attached to it.

boxes.body: A full symphony orchestra, a solo instrument, or synthesisers. The forces set the world.

boxes.title: Mode and harmony
boxes.body: Major and diatonic sounds settled; minor, chromatic or dissonant does not.

boxes.title: Tempo and rhythm
boxes.body: A march, a waltz, a driving ostinato. The pulse tells you what kind of scene this is.

boxes.title: Register and dynamics
boxes.body: High and quiet is fragile; low and loud is threat. The extremes carry meaning on their own.

An ostinato

check.solution: A **stinger**: a sudden chord or crash timed to a specific moment on screen. A leitmotif is a recurring idea tied to a character or concept; an ostinato is a repeating pattern; a cadence is the pair of chords that ends a phrase.

steps.title: Diegetic and non-diegetic
steps.body:
One question sorts all film music into two boxes, and it is worth knowing cold.

> **Can the characters hear it?**

**Diegetic** music exists inside the story. A car radio, a band in a bar, a character singing in the shower, a music box. The characters can hear it, and it usually sounds as though it is coming from somewhere in the room — often a bit muffled, or in mono, or with the acoustic of that space.

**Non-diegetic** music is the **score**: the orchestra nobody on screen can hear, playing to the audience alone. Almost all the music in most films is non-diegetic.

The distinction earns marks on its own, and it earns more when a film plays with it. Music that starts as a character's radio and swells into a full orchestral arrangement has crossed from one to the other, and the effect is to move the audience from watching a scene to feeling it.

**How to tell, when you cannot see the picture.** Diegetic music usually carries the acoustics of a real space: it sounds recorded rather than scored, it may be a complete song rather than a cue, and it often has an audible source — a piano in a room, a tinny speaker. Non-diegetic music sits cleanly across the whole soundtrack and starts and stops with the drama rather than with a door opening.

A third word occasionally appears: **underscore**, which is non-diegetic music running quietly under dialogue. It has to stay out of the way of the words, which is why underscore is typically sustained, low in the mix and thin in texture.

as if in the room, with its acoustic
a cue, shaped to the scene
a car radio, a band, a music box

check.prompt: A character switches on a radio and a song plays. Later the same song returns, played by a full orchestra, while the character is alone and silent. What has happened?
options: It has moved from diegetic to non-diegetic
It has moved from non-diegetic to diegetic
Both appearances are diegetic, since it is the same song
Neither is diegetic, because a song is not a score
check.solution: The radio is a source inside the scene, so that appearance is **diegetic**. The orchestral return has no source in the world of the film, so it is **non-diegetic**. Moving music from one to the other is a deliberate effect: it takes something the character heard and turns it into something they are feeling.

steps.title: The leitmotif
steps.body:
A **leitmotif** is a short musical idea attached to a **character, a place or an idea**, which returns when they do and changes as the story changes them.

The technique comes from **Wagner**, who used it across his operas, and it was taken into film scoring by composers working in the late-Romantic symphonic tradition. John Williams's *Star Wars* score (**1977**) is the most famous example: the main title is Luke Skywalker's theme, and it can return whenever the story turns to him.

**Three things make a leitmotif work.**

**It has to be short.** A long tune cannot be dropped into the middle of a scene. Most leitmotifs are three to seven notes.

**It has to be distinctive.** Usually one striking interval or rhythm does the work. The *Star Wars* theme opens by leaping up a **perfect fifth**, 7 semitones, which is wide, open and unmistakable, and the bars that follow drive up through triplet quavers to a leap of a **minor seventh**, 10 semitones — wider still, so the theme keeps climbing in intensity.

**It has to survive being changed.** This is the important one. A leitmotif is only useful if you can still recognise it when it is slower, quieter, in the minor, on a single horn instead of the whole brass section. That recognisability under transformation is what lets the music comment on a character rather than merely announce them.

> The same theme played slowly and quietly by a single horn means something very different from the full brass at the start — and it means it *because* you recognise it.

**In the exam.** *Leitmotif* is the term, **Wagner** is the origin, and *it can return changed* is the point. Always say what the motif is attached to.

boxes.title: Short
boxes.body: Three to seven notes. Long enough to recognise, short enough to drop into a scene.

boxes.title: Distinctive
boxes.body: One striking interval or rhythm. The Star Wars theme opens on a rising perfect fifth.

boxes.title: Attached to something
boxes.body: A character, a place, an idea. Without that it is just a tune that comes back.

boxes.title: Survives transformation
boxes.body: Still recognisable slower, quieter, in the minor, on one instrument. That is what lets it comment.

visuals.alt: Four boxes on what makes a leitmotif work as a technique

steps.title: Nine ways to develop a motif
steps.body:
When a motif returns, it almost never returns unchanged. Each of these is a named technique that can be heard and credited.

**Transposition.** The same motif starting on a different note. Every interval inside it is unchanged; only the pitch level moves. Higher usually reads as brighter or more urgent, lower as heavier.

**Sequence.** The motif repeated immediately at a different pitch, often several times in a row, climbing or falling.

**Inversion.** Every interval turned upside down: a rise of two semitones becomes a fall of two. A motif that went **up, up, down** now goes **down, down, up**. Invert an inversion and you get the original back.

**Retrograde.** The motif backwards. Reverse it twice and you have the original again.

**Augmentation.** Every note value doubled, so the motif becomes broad and slow without the beat changing.

**Diminution.** Every note value halved, so it becomes urgent and busy — again without the tempo moving.

**Fragmentation.** Only part of the motif is used, usually the most distinctive bit, repeated. This is how film composers build tension: the idea is present but never completes.

**Change of mode.** The motif moved from major to minor, or the reverse. A major and a minor triad differ in exactly **one** of their three notes, by a single semitone — a tiny change on paper and an enormous one in effect.

**Reharmonisation.** The motif is unchanged and the chords underneath it are not. The same tune over a dissonant harmony means something quite different.

And one more that is not strictly a transformation but does as much work: **a change of instrument**. The motif on a solo horn, on the full brass, on a celesta, on a distorted guitar. Same notes, different world.

one note of the triad, by a semitone

visuals.problem: A motif rises a tone, rises another tone, then falls back to where it started. Work out its inversion and its retrograde.

steps.text: As intervals in semitones the motif is 2, 2, -4.
steps.note: A rise of two semitones is a tone. The fall of four brings it back to the starting note.

steps.text: Its pitches, counted from the starting note, are 0, 2, 4, 0.
steps.note: Up a tone, up another, then back down a major third to the start.
So the pitches become 0, -2, -4, 0 — it falls where it rose, and still ends where it began.

steps.text: In retrograde the intervals come in reverse order: -4, 2, 2.
steps.note: The same notes, played backwards. Reverse it again and the original returns.

steps.text: Fragmenting it gives 2, 2 — the rising pair on its own.
steps.note: Repeating that fragment without ever completing the motif is how a composer builds tension.

check.prompt: A motif rises a tone, rises another tone, then falls. In a later scene it falls a tone, falls another tone, then rises. What has been done to it?
options: Retrograde
Transposition
Augmentation
Inversion
check.solution: **Inversion**: every interval keeps its size and reverses its direction, so 2, 2, -4 becomes -2, -2, 4. Retrograde would play the same notes backwards; transposition would move the pitch and change nothing else; augmentation would double the note values.

markScheme.description: inversion

steps.title: One motif, six scenes
steps.body:
Here is a single four-note motif, and what a composer does with it across a film. It belongs to a character.

**The motif.** Four notes. It rises a tone, rises another tone, then falls back to the note it started on. Loud, on the brass, in a major key.

That is all the material there is. Everything below is the same four notes.

**Scene 1 — the character arrives.** As written: brass, major, loud, at a moderate tempo.

**Scene 2 — they are alone at night.** The same notes on a **solo horn**, quiet, with every note value **doubled**.

**Scene 3 — they are in danger.** Only the **first two notes**, repeated over and over in the low strings, getting faster, never completing.

**Scene 4 — they are defeated.** The motif in the **minor**, on a single oboe, over a sustained dissonant chord.

**Scene 5 — an enemy is revealed.** The motif **upside down**: falling where it rose, on low brass.

**Scene 6 — they return in triumph.** The motif in the major again, on the **full orchestra**, with the note values **halved** so it drives, and a **sequence** climbing it twice more.

Work through what has been done each time before reading the table.

visuals.problem: Why is Scene 3 the most effective use of the motif in the film?

steps.text: It uses only the first two notes of the four.
That fragment is the rising pair, so it always sounds like a beginning.
steps.note: Repeating a beginning over and over promises an arrival that never comes.

steps.text: The motif therefore never resolves back to its starting note.
steps.note: The original falls back to where it began; the fragment cannot, because the falling interval has been cut off.

steps.text: So the tension is structural rather than merely loud.
steps.note: A composer could get tension from volume and dissonance. This gets it from an incomplete idea, which is why it keeps working.

check.prompt: In Scene 3 the composer repeats only the first two notes of the motif, faster and faster, never completing it. Why is that tense?
options: Repeating notes is always tense whatever the notes are
The idea keeps starting and never arrives, so nothing resolves
Two notes are harder for an audience to recognise than four
The motif has been inverted, and inversions sound unsettling
check.solution: The fragment used is the **rising** pair, which always sounds like the beginning of something. Cutting off the fall that completes the motif means the idea can never return to where it started, so the tension is built into the structure rather than laid on top with volume. Nothing has been inverted.

steps.title: The sound of a mood
steps.body:
Film composers reach for the same devices again and again, because they work. Knowing them by name turns "it sounds scary" into an answer.

**Heroic or noble.** Brass, especially trumpets and horns; wide rising intervals, above all the **perfect fifth**; a **fanfare** built from the notes of the tonic triad; **dotted rhythms** and a march-like four-four; major, diatonic harmony with clear cadences.

**Tender or innocent.** A solo woodwind, often an oboe or a flute; a **conjunct** melody that moves by step and stays within a narrow range; strings sustaining underneath; a slow tempo and a quiet dynamic; the harp.

**Tense or threatening.** A **pedal** — one note held while chords change above it; a repeating **ostinato**, especially low and fast; **dissonance**; the **tritone**, exactly half an octave, which points nowhere; **tremolo** strings; percussion; the **minor second** grinding against itself.

**Strange or unreal.** A **whole-tone** scale, which has no semitones and therefore no leading note, so nothing pulls anywhere; **chromatic** writing that slides between keys; unusual instruments such as celesta, glockenspiel or theremin; **harmonics** on strings; very high or very low registers.

**Grief.** The **minor** mode; a falling melodic line; slow harmonic rhythm; low strings; silence used deliberately.

**Chase or pursuit.** A fast **ostinato**; **syncopation**; brass stabs; percussion; a rising **sequence** to keep raising the stakes.

The important habit is to give the reason, not just the effect. *A tritone, which is exactly half an octave and so belongs to no key, which is why it sounds unresolved* is a complete point. *Scary music* is not.

check.prompt: Why does a tritone sound unresolved?
options: It is the widest interval available inside a single octave
It is exactly half an octave, so it belongs to no key strongly
It contains two notes that cannot be played at the same time
It is always dissonant because it uses a flattened seventh
check.solution: A tritone is 6 semitones, and 6 times two is 12 — exactly an octave. It divides the octave in half, so it has no strong pull towards any one key, and that rootlessness is why film composers reach for it whenever something should feel unstable. The octave, at 12 semitones, is the widest interval inside an octave.

markScheme.description: it divides the octave exactly in half, so it pulls nowhere

steps.title: Writing to picture
steps.body:
Film music is written **to a finished picture**, and that constraint shapes everything about it.

**Timing is fixed.** The cue has to begin and end where the scene does, and any moment the director wants marked has to be hit exactly. Composers work to a **click track** — a metronome pulse in the headphones — so that a bar line can be made to land on a cut.

**That is why film music has unusual phrase lengths.** A concert piece can be as long as its ideas need. A cue is as long as the scene, so a composer may need a seven-bar phrase, or a bar of five, to arrive in the right place. When you hear an irregular phrase length in a film score, that is usually why.

**The music has to leave room.** Under dialogue the score becomes **underscore**: sustained, thin, low in the mix, staying out of the frequency range of the voice. Melody under speech competes with it, so the melody waits.

**Cues have names and jobs.** The **main title** establishes the world before the story starts. **Source music** is diegetic. The **end credits** can finally be a concert piece, because nothing is happening on screen.

**Orchestral colour is decided before the notes are.** *Star Wars* being played by a full symphony orchestra was itself the decision: Williams went back to the late-Romantic symphonic sound of Golden Age Hollywood composers such as **Korngold** at a time when many films used pop scores, and the score was recorded by the **London Symphony Orchestra**. That single choice does more than any individual theme.

> Context earns only when it explains something audible. *1977* on its own earns nothing; *1977, when most films used pop scores, so a full symphony orchestra sounded deliberately old-fashioned and grand* earns.

boxes.title: Fixed length
boxes.body: The cue lasts exactly as long as the scene, whatever the music would rather do.

boxes.title: Hit points
boxes.body: Moments the director wants marked. A click track lets a bar line land on a cut.

boxes.title: Irregular phrases
boxes.body: A seven-bar phrase or a bar of five, because the arrival has to happen on a particular frame.

boxes.title: Room for dialogue
boxes.body: Under speech the score thins to underscore: sustained, low, out of the way of the voice.

visuals.alt: Four boxes on the constraints that writing music to a finished picture imposes

check.prompt: Why do film cues often have irregular phrase lengths, such as seven bars rather than eight?
options: Film composers work too quickly to write regular phrases
Irregular phrases are more interesting than regular ones
Orchestras find seven-bar phrases easier to record
The music must arrive at a particular moment on screen
check.solution: A cue is as long as the scene, and any moment the director wants marked has to be hit exactly. If a cut falls where bar eight would be halfway through, the phrase becomes seven bars. Concert music can let its phrases be as long as the ideas require; film music cannot.

steps.title: Going deeper: writing about a film cue
steps.body:
The pattern that earns is always the same: **name the feature, say what it does for the film**.

| Weak | Strong |
| --- | --- |
| The music is exciting | A fortissimo brass fanfare on the tonic triad, so the opening sounds ceremonial |
| There is a scary bit | A low ostinato under a tritone in the strings, so nothing resolves |
| The theme comes back | The theme returns inverted on low brass, recognisable and wrong at once |
| It sounds sad here | The motif moves to the minor, one semitone that darkens the character |
| Lots of instruments | Three-octave doubling in violins, violas, cellos, horns and trumpets |
| It was written in 1977 | 1977, when most films used pop scores, so a symphony orchestra sounded deliberately grand |

**Three habits of a top answer.**

**Say what the music is doing for the film before you say what the music is.** *To establish a hero before we have seen one, Williams gives the theme to high trumpets* is better than the same observation without the purpose.

**Always say what a leitmotif is attached to.** The term alone is a definition; the attachment is the analysis.

**When an idea returns, name the transformation.** Transposed, inverted, in retrograde, augmented, in diminution, fragmented, reharmonised, moved to the minor, given to a different instrument. "It comes back different" is the observation you were meant to make more precisely.

And one thing to avoid entirely: **retelling the plot**. The examiner is marking what you heard.

named features, each tied to the mood it produces
Is the music diegetic or non-diegetic?
the answer, and the evidence for it
How does the music suit the action?
the job the music is doing, then the device doing it
the same element in both, then a judgement

check.solution: It names the transformation — **inversion** — names the forces, and then says what the combination does. The sentence about the theme sounding different names no technique; the one about dramatic music names no feature at all; the one about the main character’s famous theme is a fact about the film’s reputation rather than an observation about the music.

steps.title: What to carry forward
steps.body:
- Film music **does jobs**: establishing a world, telling you how to feel, identifying a character, holding the film together, marking a moment. Name the job.
- **Diegetic** music is in the scene and the characters can hear it. **Non-diegetic** is the score, for the audience alone. **Underscore** is non-diegetic music under dialogue.
- A **leitmotif** is a short idea **tied to a character, place or idea**, from **Wagner**. Always say what it is tied to.
- Nine ways to develop a motif: **transposition, sequence, inversion, retrograde, augmentation, diminution, fragmentation, change of mode, reharmonisation** — plus a change of instrument.
- **Inversion** reverses every interval's direction; **retrograde** reverses their order. Do either twice and the original returns.
- Intervals carry meaning: a **perfect fifth** (7 semitones) is open, a **tritone** (6) is exactly half an octave and points nowhere.
- A **major** and a **minor** triad differ in **one note by one semitone** — the smallest change with the biggest effect in film scoring.
- Devices: **pedal**, **ostinato**, **tremolo**, **stinger**, **fanfare**, **whole-tone**, **chromaticism**, **mickey-mousing**.
- Music is written **to picture**, which is why phrase lengths are irregular and why underscore stays out of the way of dialogue.
- The set works are **Star Wars** (1977) and **Defying Gravity** from *Wicked*.

questions.solution: A **stinger**: a sharp chord or crash timed to a specific moment. A pedal is a held note under changing chords; an ostinato is a repeating pattern; a fanfare is a flourish, usually for brass, for ceremonial effect.

markScheme.description: a stinger

questions.prompt: A motif that rose is heard again falling, with every interval the same size but in the opposite direction. What has been done?
options: It has been transposed
It is in retrograde
It has been inverted
It has been augmented
questions.solution: **Inversion**: each interval keeps its size and reverses its direction, so 2, 2, -4 becomes -2, -2, 4. Transposition moves the whole thing to a different pitch without changing any interval; retrograde plays the notes backwards; augmentation doubles the note values.

markScheme.description: inverted

questions.prompt: A motif is heard with the same pitches but every note value doubled, at the same tempo. Name the technique and its effect.
options: Diminution: the motif becomes urgent and busy, at twice the speed
Ritardando: the tempo itself gradually slows through the passage
Augmentation: the motif becomes broad and slow, though the beat is unchanged
Inversion: the shape of the motif is turned upside down
questions.solution: Doubling every note value is **augmentation**. The motif takes twice as long to unfold and sounds broad, but the pulse underneath has not altered — that is the distinction from a ritardando, which slows the beat itself. Diminution is the opposite; inversion changes direction, not duration.

markScheme.description: augmentation, broad and slow at the same tempo

questions.prompt: A composer uses only the first two notes of a motif, repeating them without ever completing the idea. Give the term for this.
questions.solution: **Fragmentation**: using only part of a motif, usually the most distinctive part. It is a standard way of building tension, because an idea that keeps starting and never arrives cannot resolve, so the tension is structural rather than merely loud.

markScheme.description: fragmentation

questions.prompt: What makes a tritone useful to a film composer who wants a scene to feel unstable?
options: It is dissonant because the two notes are only one semitone apart
It divides the octave exactly in half, so it belongs to no key strongly
It is the largest interval that can be played on most instruments
It can only be played by brass instruments, which sound threatening
questions.solution: A tritone is 6 semitones, and 6 doubled is 12 — an octave exactly. Because it splits the octave evenly it has no strong pull towards any one key, and that rootlessness is what composers use. Two notes a semitone apart make a **minor second**, which is a different interval.

markScheme.description: it splits the octave in half, so it pulls nowhere

questions.prompt: A film score changes a character’s theme from major to minor. How many notes of the triad have actually changed, and by how much?
options: Two notes, by one semitone each
All three notes, by a semitone each
One note, by one semitone
One note, by a whole tone
questions.solution: A major triad is root, 4 semitones, 7 semitones; a minor triad is root, 3, 7. Only the **third** moves, and it moves by **one semitone**. It is the smallest change available and among the largest in effect, which is why film composers use it constantly.

markScheme.description: one note, by one semitone

questions.prompt: Name the composer whose operas the leitmotif technique comes from.
questions.solution: **Wagner**, who developed the technique across his operas. John Williams took it into film scoring along with the late-Romantic symphonic sound of Golden Age Hollywood composers such as Korngold, which is why the *Star Wars* score works as it does.

markScheme.description: Wagner

questions.prompt: Why is a cue in a film often an unusual number of bars long, such as 23?
options: Film composers do not count bars while they are writing
It has to start and finish exactly where the scene does
Odd numbers of bars sound more interesting to an audience
The orchestra is paid by the bar, so cues are kept short
questions.solution: Music written to picture is as long as the picture. Any moment the director wants marked has to be hit exactly, so a phrase may have to be seven bars rather than eight, or a bar of five may appear, in order to arrive on the right frame. Concert music has no such constraint.

markScheme.description: the cue must fit the length of the scene

questions.prompt: A composer introduces a hero’s leitmotif and develops it across a film. Put these treatments into the order that tells the story most effectively.
items: State it plainly on the brass, loud, in the major
Give it to a solo horn, quiet, with the note values doubled
Use only its opening fragment, repeating and never completing it
Move it into the minor over a dissonant chord
Return it on the full orchestra, in the major, with the values halved
questions.solution: The plain statement has to come first, because nothing can be recognised as a transformation until the original is known. The quiet solo version reads as isolation, the incomplete fragment as danger, and the minor as defeat — each further from the original than the last. The full orchestral return in the major, faster, is a triumph only because of everything it is being compared with. The order is the dramatic arc.

markScheme.description: the plain statement first
the fragment and the minor version in the middle, as the low points
the full orchestral major return last

questions.prompt: A motif is played with its notes in reverse order. What is that called, and what happens if you do it twice?
options: Retrograde, and doing it twice gives the original motif back
Inversion, and doing it twice gives the original motif back
Retrograde, and doing it twice reverses the intervals as well
Transposition, and doing it twice moves it up two steps
questions.solution: Playing the notes backwards is **retrograde**: 2, 2, -4 becomes -4, 2, 2. Reverse that again and you have 2, 2, -4 — the original. Inversion is a different operation, turning every interval upside down, and it too returns the original if applied twice.

markScheme.description: retrograde, and twice returns the original

questions.prompt: Which use of context would earn in an answer about the Star Wars main title?
options: It was composed in 1977 by John Williams for a film that was directed by George Lucas
It is one of the most widely recognisable pieces of film music ever to have been written
The score has been performed in concert halls all over the world in the years since then
Written when many films used pop scores, so a symphony orchestra sounded deliberately grand
questions.solution: Context earns when it explains something **audible**. Knowing that most films of the period used pop scores is what makes the choice of a full symphony orchestra meaningful rather than merely a fact. A date, a director and a reputation explain nothing you can hear.

markScheme.description: the option connecting the date to why the orchestral sound was a choice

questions.prompt: A theme opens by leaping up a perfect fifth and later leaps up a minor seventh. How many semitones wider is the second leap than the first?
questions.solution: A perfect fifth is 7 semitones and a minor seventh is 10, so the second leap is **3** semitones wider. That widening is deliberate: each leap opens further than the last, so the theme keeps climbing in intensity rather than settling after its first gesture.

markScheme.description: 10 minus 7 = 3

questions.prompt:
A cue from a film is played several times, with a skeleton score showing the leading melodic line.

**On the page:** no sharps or flats; four crotchets in a bar. The cue is 23 bars long, which is not a multiple of four or eight.

**What you hear:**

- Bars 1 to 6: a solo oboe plays a five-note idea, quiet, moving entirely by step within a fifth, over sustained strings.
- Bars 7 to 12: the same five notes on a solo horn, an octave lower, with every note value doubled.
- Bars 13 to 18: only the first two notes of the idea, repeated in the low strings under a held note that never changes, getting faster each time and never completing the idea.
- Bars 19 to 22: the five notes return on the full brass, loud, with every note value halved, and the harmony now falls on the minor rather than the major.
- Bar 23: a single loud orchestral chord, cut off immediately.

Describe how the composer develops the five-note idea across this cue, naming the technique used in each section and saying what it contributes to the scene.
questions.solution:
**Bars 1 to 6: the idea stated plainly.** Five notes on a solo oboe, quiet, moving entirely **by step** — **conjunct** — and staying within a **fifth**. A narrow, stepwise line on a single reed instrument is the standard sound of tenderness or innocence in film scoring, and stating it plainly first is necessary: nothing later can be heard as a transformation unless the original is known.

**Bars 7 to 12: augmentation, with a change of instrument and register.** The same five notes appear on a **solo horn an octave lower**, with every note value **doubled**. Doubling the values is **augmentation**, and the beat has not changed — the idea simply takes twice as long to unfold, so it sounds broad rather than slow. Moving it down an octave and onto a horn darkens and warms it. Same notes, different world.

**Bars 13 to 18: fragmentation over a pedal.** Only the **first two notes** are used, repeated in the low strings and accelerating. That is **fragmentation**, and it is the most effective passage in the cue, because the fragment chosen is the *opening* of the idea and therefore always sounds like a beginning. Repeating a beginning that never arrives means nothing can resolve, so the tension is built into the structure rather than laid on with volume. Underneath it a **pedal** — one note held while everything above changes — adds a second layer of unresolved harmony.

**Bars 19 to 22: diminution and a change of mode.** The five notes return on **full brass, fortissimo**, with every value **halved** — **diminution**, so the idea is now urgent and driving at the same tempo. At the same time the harmony falls on the **minor**. A major and a minor triad differ in only **one note by one semitone**, and that single semitone turns the character’s own theme against them. Combining it with the loudest possible orchestration means the return is overwhelming rather than reassuring.

**Bar 23: a stinger.** One loud chord, cut off immediately, timed to a moment on screen.

**Two further observations.** The cue is **non-diegetic**: there is no source in the scene and it moves with the drama rather than with anything visible. And it is **23 bars** long — not a multiple of four or eight — which is characteristic of music written **to picture**, where the cue has to start and finish where the scene does and hit particular frames on the way.

**Overall.** One five-note idea supplies the whole cue, and its four appearances trace an arc: stated, isolated, threatened, overwhelmed. Nothing new is introduced at any point, which is exactly why the transformations register.

bars 13 to 18 identified as fragmentation

identifies the cue as non-diegetic and 23 bars as writing to picture

questions.prompt:
A main title cue is played several times, with a skeleton score showing the melody and chord symbols above it.

**On the page:** three flats in the key signature; four crotchets in a bar; a fast tempo. The melody begins and ends on E flat. The chord symbols printed for bars 9 to 16 are E♭ | Cm | A♭ | B♭7 | E♭ | Cm | A♭ | B♭7.

**What you hear:**

- Bars 1 to 8: trumpets and horns in octaves, fortissimo, using only the notes E flat, G and B flat, in dotted rhythms, over a snare drum.
- Bars 9 to 16: the violins take a long melody; it opens by leaping up seven semitones from E flat to B flat, then drives up through triplet quavers to a leap of ten semitones.
- Bars 17 to 24: the bars 9 to 16 melody again, doubled across three octaves in violins, violas, cellos, horns and trumpets.
- Bars 25 to 30: the first three notes of the melody only, repeated three times, each time a tone higher than the last.
- Bar 31: a cymbal crash and a long final chord.

Analyse how this main title establishes a heroic mood, referring to instrumentation, melody, harmony and the way the material is developed.
questions.solution:
**Instrumentation.** The cue opens with **trumpets and horns in octaves at a fortissimo dynamic** over a snare drum, using only the notes **E flat, G and B flat** — the notes of the tonic triad. Brass in octaves is the loudest, most penetrating sound an orchestra has and carries no harmony of its own, so the opening reads as a **fanfare**: a summons rather than a tune. Brass has been the sound of ceremony and heroism for centuries, so the audience hears a hero before seeing one. At bar 17 the melody is **doubled across three octaves** in violins, violas, cellos, horns and trumpets, which is simply the largest sound available and is saved for the return rather than spent at the start.

**Melody.** The violin melody at bar 9 opens by leaping **up seven semitones**, from E flat to B flat — a **perfect fifth**. A wide, open rising interval sounds bold and confident in a way a step cannot, and the fifth in particular is the interval on which the tonic and dominant of a key sit, so it sounds settled as well as broad. The melody then drives up through **triplet quavers** to a leap of **ten semitones**, a **minor seventh** — 3 semitones wider than the first. That widening is the point: each gesture opens further than the last, so the theme keeps climbing rather than settling after its opening leap.

**Harmony.** Three flats with the melody beginning and ending on E flat gives **E flat major**. The printed chords read straight off as roman numerals: E flat is **I**, C minor is **vi**, A flat is **IV**, B flat 7 is **V7**. That is an entirely **functional, diatonic** progression with no chromatic chords at all, which is what makes the passage sound confident rather than uneasy — a hero introduced over unstable harmony would not read as a hero. The four chords fill bars 9 to 12 and then repeat for 13 to 16, so the whole melody sits on a **repeated chord pattern**, and that repetition lets the ear expect the arrival at bar 17 before it happens.

**Rhythm.** **Dotted rhythms** run through the opening fanfare. Dotted rhythms are the rhythm of a march and of a military fanfare, and in a steady four-four they give the music the character of marching — which is what heroes do. The **triplet quavers** in the melody push the phrase forward across the beat instead of letting it settle.

**Development.** At bars 25 to 30 the composer uses **only the first three notes** of the melody, repeated three times, each a tone higher than the last. Using part of an idea is **fragmentation**, and repeating it at rising pitch levels is a **rising sequence**. A sequence that climbs raises the tessitura of every part, which is heard as increasing effort and brightness, so the cue gains intensity without any new material at all. The **cymbal crash** and long final chord at bar 31 close it.

**Overall.** Nothing here is subtle, and that is the point of a main title: it has to establish a world before the story starts, often over nothing but a caption. A fanfare on the tonic triad, dotted rhythms, entirely functional harmony, an opening interval as wide and open as a perfect fifth, three-octave doubling at the return and a rising sequence at the end — every device is a familiar signal, and all of them point the same way.

the three-octave doubling at bar 17
identifies the opening leap as a perfect fifth
identifies the second leap as a minor seventh and says it is wider
identifies E flat major from the signature and the final note
reads the chords as I, vi, IV and V7
identifies the dotted rhythms as march-like
identifies fragmentation and a rising sequence at bars 25 to 30

Melody: identifies the leaps as a perfect fifth and a minor seventh, and their effect
Harmony: reads E flat major from the signature and final note, and the chords as I, vi, IV, V7

questions.prompt: Non-diegetic music playing quietly under dialogue is usually sustained, thin and low in the mix. Why?
options: Composers write less carefully for quiet passages
Thin textures are cheaper to record with an orchestra
Sustained music is easier to synchronise with the picture
It has to stay out of the way of the voices
questions.solution: This is **underscore**, and its job is to colour a scene without competing with the words. A melody under speech pulls attention away from the dialogue, and music sitting in the same frequency range as the voice masks it, so underscore is typically sustained, thin, and out of the way. The constraint shapes the writing.

markScheme.description: it must not compete with the dialogue

questions.prompt: Which observation about a returning leitmotif would earn the most?
options: It returns inverted on low brass, so it is recognisable and wrong at once
It returns later in the film, sounding rather different from before
It returns and reminds the audience of the character it belongs to
It returns because the composer wanted to use the material again
questions.solution: It names the **transformation**, names the **forces**, and then says what the combination achieves. Sounding rather different names no technique; reminding the audience of the character is true of every leitmotif and so says nothing about this one; the composer wanting to reuse material is a claim about intentions rather than an observation about the music.

markScheme.description: the option naming the transformation, the forces and the effect

questions.prompt: Explain how a film composer can use a single short motif to follow a character through a whole film, naming at least five ways the motif can be changed and saying what each change can be made to mean.
questions.solution:
**The idea.** A **leitmotif** is a short musical idea attached to a character, a place or an idea, which returns when they do and changes as the story changes them. The technique comes from **Wagner** and reached film scoring through composers working in the late-Romantic symphonic tradition.

**Why it has to be built a certain way.** Three things make a leitmotif usable. It has to be **short** — three to seven notes — so it can be dropped into the middle of a scene. It has to be **distinctive**, usually through one striking interval or rhythm. And above all it has to remain **recognisable when it is changed**, because a motif that is only identifiable in its original form can announce a character but cannot say anything about them.

**Augmentation.** Every note value doubled, so the motif unfolds at half its former rate although the beat is untouched. Broad and unhurried. Dramatically this reads as weight, memory or calm, and on a solo instrument it reads as isolation.

**Diminution.** Every note value halved, so the motif becomes urgent and driving at the same tempo. Used for pursuit, for resolve, and for a triumphant return where the character is doing rather than being.

**Fragmentation.** Only part of the motif — usually its opening — repeated and never completed. This is the most powerful of all for tension, because the fragment always sounds like a beginning and a beginning that never arrives cannot resolve. The tension is structural rather than merely loud, which is why it can be sustained for minutes without wearing out.

**Change of mode.** Major to minor. A major and a minor triad differ in exactly **one** of their three notes, by a **single semitone** — the smallest change available and among the largest in effect. The same theme, one note different, turns a character’s own music against them.

**Inversion.** Every interval keeps its size and reverses its direction, so a motif that rose now falls. Because the sizes survive, it stays recognisable while being audibly wrong, which suits a corrupted version of a character or an enemy who mirrors them.

**Retrograde, reharmonisation and orchestration.** Retrograde plays the notes backwards; reharmonisation leaves the motif untouched and changes the chords underneath it, so a familiar tune arrives somewhere unexpected; and simply moving the motif from full brass to a single oboe, or from high strings to low, changes its meaning without altering a note.

**Why the technique works at all.** Every one of these depends on the audience knowing the original, which is why a film states a leitmotif plainly the first time and only then begins to work on it. What the audience is following is not the notes but the **relationship** between what they are hearing and what they remember. That is why a fragment can be frightening, why one semitone can be devastating, and why a theme returning on the full orchestra at the end of a film feels earned rather than merely loud. The composer has spent the whole film making the audience care about four notes.

examTechnique.body:
**This is Area of Study 3, Music for Stage and Screen.** The set works are John Williams's *Star Wars* main title (**1977**) and Stephen Schwartz's *Defying Gravity* from *Wicked*. An unfamiliar Section A extract could be a cue from any film in a similar style.

**Say what the music is doing for the film.** Film music has jobs — establishing a place or period, telling you how to feel, identifying a character, covering a cut. Naming the job is half of any answer here.

**Diegetic or non-diegetic?** Can the characters hear it? That single question is worth knowing cold.

**Name the motif and what it is attached to.** *A leitmotif* on its own is not an answer; *Luke's leitmotif, given to the brass* is.

**When a motif returns, say how it has changed.** Higher, lower, slower, faster, minor, fragmented, on a different instrument, harmonised differently. Each of those is a nameable technique.

**Intervals carry meaning.** A perfect fifth is open; a tritone is unstable; a minor second is anxious. Say the interval and then the effect.

**Orchestral colour is the composer's fastest tool.** Brass for ceremony and heroism, strings for warmth or tension, high woodwind for innocence, low strings and percussion for threat, unusual instruments for strangeness.

**Context earns when it explains the sound.** Williams revived the late-Romantic symphonic style of Golden Age Hollywood composers such as Korngold at a time when many films used pop scores, and the *Star Wars* score was recorded by the London Symphony Orchestra.
examinerErrors: Calling any recurring tune a leitmotif without saying what it is tied to.
Saying a motif "comes back different" without naming the transformation.
Describing the feeling — tense, exciting, sad — with no musical feature attached.
Muddling diegetic and non-diegetic, or never mentioning the distinction at all.
Naming the instrument family rather than the instrument: "brass" where "muted trumpet" was wanted.
Treating a change of key and a change of mode as the same thing.
Retelling the plot of the film instead of describing the music.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer says what the music is doing for the film before it says what the music is, then supports every claim from the score. It knows a leitmotif is a motif tied to something and always says what. When an idea returns it names the transformation — inverted, in retrograde, augmented, fragmented, reharmonised, moved to the minor — rather than saying it has changed. It reads meaning from intervals and from orchestration rather than from atmosphere, and it can explain why a fifth sounds open and a tritone does not. And it uses context only where the context explains something audible.
